hints: Each value must occur n times, so swapping entries preserves that requirement.
Build a grid whose row sums and column sums are each already distinct.
For n>4, the initial grid has one row-column sum collision; two carefully chosen swaps eliminate it.
analogy: Start with two sets of distinct labels for row and column totals, then repair their single overlap without changing how often any value appears.
example: For n=4, rows [2,1,2,1], [4,2,4,3], [3,3,4,4], [3,2,1,1] use each value four times. Their row sums 6,13,14,7 and column sums 12,8,11,9 are all different.
algorithm: For n<=3 print IMPOSSIBLE; for n=4 use the example grid. For n>4, use one-based indices and set A[i,1]=n, A[i,j]=i when j>i, and A[i,j]=i-1 otherwise. Compute row sums R[i]=2n-1+(n-2)(i-1), column sum C[1]=n^2, and C[j]=n(n-1)/2+j-1 for j>=2. Find the unique collision R[i]=C[j], j>=2. Swap A[2,1] with A[2,j], then swap A[i+1,n] with A[i+2,n]. Print the grid.
correctness: In the initial grid each value occurs n times. Row sums increase by n-2, and columns 2 through n increase by one, while column 1 is largest. For n>4 these sequences have exactly one collision, away from the last two rows and end columns. The first swap increases the colliding column by n-2; the second adjusts the next two row sums by +1 and -1, removing the newly created collision without creating another. Swaps preserve all frequencies. The small cases can be checked exhaustively.
complexity: For grid side n, O(n^2) time and O(n^2) space to build and print the grid.
